mcqs.question: What is the test for whether a seam is "cheap enough" to build before a second use case exists?
options: Whether it was requested by a senior engineer
Whether removing it later, if it turns out to be unneeded, would cost more than a few minutes
Whether it uses an interface rather than a concrete class, regardless of size
Whether the team has more than a week of slack in the current sprint
mcqs.explanation: The actual bar is cheap to build AND cheap to undo — if deleting an unused seam later would take more than a few minutes, it wasn't cheap in the first place. Who requested it, whether it's an interface, and current sprint slack don't determine whether the investment was justified.

mcqs.question: A generic plugin framework was built speculatively before a second payment provider existed. When the second provider finally arrives, it needs a retry hook the framework never anticipated. What does this illustrate?
options: That the upfront speculative investment didn't buy the flexibility it was built for, since the real variation still had to be bolted on awkwardly
That plugin frameworks are always the wrong choice regardless of context
That retry logic should never be added to any payment integration
That the second payment provider was implemented incorrectly
mcqs.explanation: Guessing at a future shape without real examples usually guesses wrong — the framework's investment gets spent on flexibility that isn't what's actually needed, and the real variation gets bolted on anyway. This isn't a blanket case against plugin frameworks or a criticism of the specific implementation; it's about the timing and evidence behind the abstraction.

mcqs.question: What's the cheap insurance you can add today without building a full abstraction, that makes adding a real interface later much easier?
options: Writing exhaustive documentation for every possible future variant
Adding the plugin framework immediately regardless of current need
Keeping payment-gateway calls isolated behind one module boundary today, rather than scattered through business logic, so an interface can be added there localized later
Refusing to write any code until the second use case is confirmed
mcqs.explanation: A clean boundary costs little today and makes the eventual interface a localized change rather than a hunt through scattered call sites. Exhaustive docs for unknown futures and building the framework immediately both invest in speculation; refusing to write code isn't a realistic option either.

mcqs.question: Why is building a fully generic plugin framework "just in case" before a second real use case exists considered the wrong call?
options: Because plugin frameworks are never appropriate in any codebase
Because YAGNI forbids writing any interfaces at all
Because generic frameworks always run slower than direct implementations
Because the framework's shape is a guess made with zero real examples, and the real second case rarely fits the imagined shape
mcqs.explanation: Without a real second example, the shape of the abstraction is pure guesswork, and guesses about future variation are usually wrong — the actual second case tends to need something the imagined framework didn't anticipate. This isn't a performance argument, a blanket ban on frameworks, or a ban on interfaces generally — cheap seams for known needs are still fine.
